unit.unitOverview: Unit 9 is about scripts: the writing that actors follow on a stage and in front of a camera. You will read “The Forest Guardians” first as a play script and then as a film script, comparing stage directions with camera directions such as pan, zoom and close-up. You will also study compound nouns like woodland, footpath and bamboo grove, and write and perform a short scene of your own. The unit story, “Nookwatch: The Forest Mission”, follows Amal and Sami as they help rescue an injured lemur at a woodland rescue centre.
unit.learningPath:
1. Vocabulary: learn the twenty-five unit words in five groups, a few each day.
2. Reading: read “The Forest Guardians” as a play script, then the same scene as a film script.
3. Story: read “Nookwatch: The Forest Mission” in its three parts.
4. Comprehension: answer the twelve questions on the passages you have read.
5. Grammar: work through the six compound-noun lessons and their practice parts.
6. Writing: complete the six writing tasks, beginning with your own play script scene.
7. Speaking: perform, direct and record the six speaking activities.
8. Activities: finish the six exercises, then take the checkpoint quiz.
9. My progress: rate yourself on the six self-assessment statements.

readings.title: The Forest Guardians: a play script
readings.setting: A woodland animal rescue centre near Fort Portal
readings.passageScript:
THE FOREST GUARDIANS
A play in one scene

CHARACTERS:
NARRATOR — tells the audience what is happening
AMAL — a student who cares deeply about animals
SAMI — a student who loves exploring the woodland
TALIA — the vet who leads the Nookwatch rescue centre
TEACHER YASMIN — the class teacher from Hilltop Primary

SETTING: A clearing beside a bamboo forest. A wooden shelter stands upstage right, and a footpath leads into the trees downstage left.

NARRATOR: [Stands centre stage, holding a clipboard] It is early morning, and mist still hangs over the bamboo grove. Two students have arrived at the Nookwatch Animal Rescue Centre for their first day.

[AMAL and SAMI enter downstage left, carrying notebooks. TEACHER YASMIN follows them.]

AMAL: [Looking around in wonder] This place is beautiful. I can hear birds calling from every direction.

SAMI: [Pointing upstage] Look at that bamboo grove. The guidebook says gibbons swing between the tall stems.

TALIA: [Enters upstage right, wearing a green hat] Welcome, both of you. I am the vet here, and this is no zoo.

TEACHER YASMIN: [Smiling] They have read the animal-care manual twice already, and they made a checklist.

TALIA: Good teamwork. Today our oldest lemur, Kobi, is missing from his sleeping nook.

SAMI: [Opening his notebook] What does he look like?

TALIA: He has dark eyes and thick brown fur, soft as a woven textile.

AMAL: Where was he last seen?

TALIA: [Pointing downstage left] Near the footpath by the bamboo grove. I found strange footprints there this morning.

SAMI: [Kneeling and examining the ground] These prints look abnormal. His back foot seems twisted.

AMAL: [Worried] Then we must tell you the moment we spot another one.

TEACHER YASMIN: Mark the trail with this tape, and write down exactly what you see.

[AMAL ties tape to a low branch. SAMI sketches the footprints in his notebook. TALIA exits upstage right.]

NARRATOR: [Stepping forward] The students worked quickly and carefully. By lunchtime the search team had found Kobi resting in the bamboo grove, tired but safe.

[TALIA enters downstage right, carrying a first-aid kit.]

TALIA: [To SAMI] Good work spotting those prints. You may have saved Kobi's life.

SAMI: [Standing proudly] We simply followed the manual and used our eyes.

AMAL: Caring for woodland creatures is everyone's duty, and together we can protect this whole forest.

NARRATOR: [Stepping forward] And so the Forest Guardians began their mission: one footprint, one creature, one act of kindness at a time.

[ALL bow. CURTAIN.]

readings.title: Nookwatch: The Forest Mission, part 1
readings.setting: The Nookwatch Animal Rescue Centre and its bamboo forest
readings.passageScript:
In the hills outside Fort Portal, near the edge of a sprawling bamboo forest, stood the Nookwatch Animal Rescue Centre. It was a peaceful place where injured woodland creatures were treated and slowly returned to the wild. The rescue team called themselves the “Rangers of the Grove”.
Year 5 students from Hilltop Primary had come for a one-week project. “This is no zoo,” said Talia, the vet who leads the centre, “so you must stay alert. You will observe, assist and report on animal behaviour.”
Amal looked around at the woodland paths, the high trees and the small shaded corners. “Where is our first stop?”
“The lemur habitat,” said Talia. “One of the grooves in the tree was found empty this morning. It was the favourite sleeping nook of Kobi, our oldest lemur.”
The students grabbed notebooks and followed Talia into the clearing. “We will assemble every clue,” she said. “Look for prints, dropped food or signs of illness. Check the manual in the visitor cabin if you forget something.”
Sami opened the guidebook. “It says lemurs love to climb, but they rarely travel far alone.”
“Then we should check behind the capsule shelter,” said Amal. “It is warm and dry, so he might be hiding there.”
They tiptoed towards the shelter and found a line of footprints. Sami leaned close. “These prints are abnormal. His back foot looks twisted.”
“We must alert Talia,” said Amal, “and mark this path with tape.”
Later that day Talia met them beside the lemur trail. “Good job spotting this,” she said. “Animals rarely show signs of injury unless it is serious.”
She paused and pointed at a small dimple in the mud. “That is a pawprint too, which means Kobi had company.”

readings.title: Nookwatch: The Forest Mission, part 2
readings.setting: The monkey habitat and the shelter the students help to build
readings.passageScript:
“You mean another animal?” asked Amal.
“Possibly,” said Talia. “Or a person. Nobody should be near the enclosures without permission.”
That evening the group helped clean the monkey habitat. They raked leaves and refilled the feeders with edible fruit. “You should avoid feeding wild animals by hand,” Talia reminded them. “They must not forget how to search for their own food.”
Amal swept the path gently. “These creatures have their own style. Even the way they move is full of character.”
Sami nodded. “I love the gibbons. The baby one has thick fur, like a brown textile coat.”
Talia smiled. “And it is very durable. Nature protects its own whenever it can.”
The next morning the news spread through the centre. “We have found Kobi,” called Talia. “He is safe, but limping. He was in the bamboo grove, eating slowly.”
“Will he recover?” Amal asked.
“Yes,” Talia replied, “but he will need ample rest and a new capsule shelter closer to the main path.”
While they were building the shelter, Sami said, “We have read about animals in textbooks, but seeing them is completely different.”
Amal agreed. “It feels more real, and more urgent. You cannot stay neutral once you have seen them up close.”
By day three the class was helping with new research tasks. Amal chose to observe maternal behaviour among the red-tailed monkeys. “The mothers are gentle but watchful,” she noted. “One cradled her baby as though it were wrapped in gold.”
“Describe the paternal care too,” said Teacher Yasmin. “See how that male keeps watch? It is part of their nature.”
Sami helped the rangers repair the fences. “These materials are economical and strong,” said Talia. “We reuse whatever we can.”

readings.title: Nookwatch: The Forest Mission, part 3
readings.setting: The centre's final days, from the lunch table to the news skit
readings.passageScript:
“Because the forest is not endless,” said Sami. “Even fertile land can lose its life.”
At lunchtime the group discussed a new case.
“There is an injured bush baby in the woods,” said Talia. “It may have fallen into a hunting trap.”
“We have to stop those traps,” said Amal. “Why are they still allowed?”
“Some people are in denial about the harm they cause,” Talia replied. “They say it is tradition.”
“But traditions must change when animals are suffering,” said Sami.

That evening the group prepared posters for their final presentations. One board said:
CRITICAL: stop snares before more animals are lost.
Informal patrols help, and students can join them.
Protect our woodland, and defend this treasure of biodiversity.
Another group made a Save the Species mural with a rhyme:
A panda with bamboo, a kangaroo too.
Do not let our forests lose their crew!
Amal and Sami wrote their own verse:
A nook is a home. A groove is a path.
An economical fix can save us from wrath.
Maternal love and paternal guard —
every creature must be starred.
On the final day the students performed a short news skit.

SAMI: Rangers report that it is healing. It had a bruised paw and a cut near its tail.
AMAL: Local families now say they are willing to build better fences.
SAMI: If that is true, it is a durable step forward.
The crowd clapped, and Talia stepped forward.

grammar.title: What a Compound Noun Is
grammar.explanation: A compound noun joins two or more words so that together they name one single thing. Knowing the parts lets you work out a new word without reaching for a dictionary every time.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
A compound noun is a noun built from two or more words that together create one new meaning.
woodland = wood + land, so it names land that is covered with trees.
textbook = text + book, so it names a book of texts for studying.
footprint = foot + print, so it names the mark that a foot leaves behind.
guidebook = guide + book, so it names a book that guides you.
clipboard = clip + board, so it names a board with a clip for holding papers.
bamboo grove = bamboo + grove, so it names a small group of bamboo plants.
first-aid kit = first-aid + kit, so it names a kit for treating injuries quickly.
Compound nouns make your writing precise. The phrase 'a woodland creature' says in two words what 'a creature that lives in the woods' takes six words to say.
grammar.commonMistake: It is easy to treat every two-word phrase as a compound noun. The phrase 'tall tree' only describes a tree, while 'bamboo grove' names one particular place, so only the second one is a compound noun.
grammar.memoryTip: Ask yourself whether the two words together name one thing. If the answer is yes, you are almost certainly looking at a compound noun.
grammar.practice:
Part A: split each compound noun into its two parts: woodland, textbook, footprint, guidebook, clipboard.
Part B: explain in one sentence what each of those compounds means, using the meaning of its parts.
Part C: rewrite each phrase as a single compound noun: a print made by a foot; a book that guides you; a board with a clip.

Answer key — Part A: woodland = wood + land; textbook = text + book; footprint = foot + print; guidebook = guide + book; clipboard = clip + board. Part B: woodland names land that is covered with trees; textbook names a book of texts for studying; footprint names the mark that a foot leaves behind; guidebook names a book that guides you; clipboard names a board with a clip for holding papers. Part C: a print made by a foot = footprint; a book that guides you = guidebook; a board with a clip = clipboard.

grammar.title: Three Types of Compound Noun
grammar.explanation: Compound nouns are written in three forms: closed, open and hyphenated. Custom fixes the form rather than a rule, so wide reading and a dictionary are your best guides.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Closed form joins the words with no space: textbook, woodland, footprint, toothbrush, clipboard, cupboard, guidebook, downstage.
Open form keeps the words separate although they still name one thing: bamboo forest, bamboo grove, stage direction, ice cream, bus stop, wildlife reserve.
Hyphenated form links the words with a short line called a hyphen: first-aid, close-up, mother-in-law, well-being.
No rule predicts the form. Many open compounds slowly close up as people use them more often, which is how 'to-day' turned into 'today'.
grammar.commonMistake: Guessing the form from the sound leads writers astray, because 'ice cream' and 'icecream' sound exactly the same when spoken. Check a dictionary whenever you are unsure, and keep a list of the forms you meet.
grammar.memoryTip: Sort every new compound into one of three boxes the moment you meet it: closed, open or hyphenated. Sorting fixes the spelling in your memory.
grammar.practice:

Answer key — Part A: closed = toothpaste, footpath, guidebook, cupboard; open = bamboo forest, ice cream, stage direction; hyphenated = well-being, mother-in-law, close-up. Part B is open-ended, since any true sentence using a Part A compound in the right form is correct — model examples: closed: 'We followed the footpath through the trees.' open: 'The bamboo forest was quiet at dawn.' hyphenated: 'The photo showed a close-up of the lemur's face.' Part C is also open-ended, since the play script contains several compound nouns to choose from — model example: 'clipboard' (closed, from '[holding a clipboard]') and 'first-aid kit' (hyphenated + open, from 'carrying a first-aid kit'); other correct choices include 'downstage' (closed) and 'bamboo grove' (open).

grammar.title: How Compound Nouns Are Built
grammar.explanation: The two halves of a compound noun can come from different word classes, and the first half normally carries the stronger stress when the word is spoken aloud.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Noun + noun: text + book = textbook, tooth + brush = toothbrush, foot + print = footprint.
Adjective + noun: wild + life = wildlife, black + board = blackboard.
Verb + noun: guide + book = guidebook, break + fast = breakfast.
Noun + verb: sun + rise = sunrise, rain + fall = rainfall.
Preposition + noun: down + stage = downstage, up + stage = upstage, under + growth = undergrowth.
Stress carries meaning. GREENhouse, stressed on GREEN, names a glass building for growing plants, while green HOUSE, stressed on HOUSE, simply describes a house painted green.
grammar.commonMistake: Stressing the second half turns a compound noun back into a plain description, so a listener hears 'black BIRD' as any bird that happens to be black rather than the blackbird singing on the rooftop.
grammar.memoryTip: Say the compound aloud and tap the table on the louder part. The tap lands on the first word almost every time.
grammar.practice:

Answer key — Part A: tooth + paste = toothpaste; rain + fall = rainfall; sun + rise = sunrise; black + board = blackboard; wild + life = wildlife. Part B: toothpaste = noun + noun; rainfall = noun + verb; sunrise = noun + verb; blackboard = adjective + noun; wildlife = adjective + noun. Part C: the stress falls on the first word in every case — TOOTHpaste, RAINfall, SUNrise, BLACKboard, WILDlife.

grammar.title: Common Mistakes with Compound Nouns
grammar.explanation: Most compound-noun errors come from splitting a closed form, joining an open form, dropping a hyphen, or adding the plural -s in the wrong place.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Splitting a closed form: 'I read my text book' should be 'I read my textbook'.
Joining an open form: 'We walked into the bambooforest' should be 'We walked into the bamboo forest'.
Dropping a hyphen: 'The close up shot was amazing' should be 'The close-up shot was amazing'.
Plurals: most compounds simply add -s at the end, giving textbooks, footprints and clipboards.
Hyphenated compounds add -s to the main noun, so mother-in-law becomes mothers-in-law, while close-up becomes close-ups because up is not the main noun.
grammar.commonMistake: The plural catches out even careful writers, who often produce 'mother-in-laws'. Ask which word names the person or the thing, then add the -s to that word.
grammar.memoryTip: Read your sentence back slowly and look at each compound twice: once for the join, and once for the plural ending.

grammar.title: Building New Compound Nouns and Reviewing the Unit
grammar.explanation: Once you know how compounds are built you can work out ones you have never met before, and this final lesson also gathers everything the unit has taught about them.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Build the meaning from the parts:
rain + coat = raincoat, a coat that keeps the rain off you.
sun + flower = sunflower, a flower that turns towards the sun.
book + shelf = bookshelf, a shelf for keeping books on.
bed + room = bedroom, a room with a bed in it.
water + fall = waterfall, water that falls from a high place.
Review of the whole unit:
A compound noun joins two or more words into one new meaning.
It appears in three forms: closed (toothbrush), open (bus stop) and hyphenated (close-up).
It can be built from noun + noun, adjective + noun, verb + noun, noun + verb or preposition + noun.
The first word usually carries the stress.
Most plurals add -s at the end, but hyphenated forms add -s to the main noun.
grammar.commonMistake: Inventing a compound that English does not actually use, such as 'sleeproom' instead of bedroom, happens easily. Build the meaning first, then check that the word really exists before you use it in your writing.
grammar.memoryTip: Treat the two words as partners sharing one job, in the same way that Amal and Sami shared one job at the rescue centre.

writing.promptAndInstructions:
Write a play script scene of eight to twelve lines of dialogue.

items: EXT. WOODLAND FOOTPATH – DUSK
WIDE-ANGLE SHOT of the footpath behind Hilltop Primary as RAVI and MINA walk into frame.
RAVI: Something has flattened the ferns just there.
PAN down to a CLOSE-UP of the strange marks in the mud. SOUND: dry leaves crunching underfoot.
MINA: That is not a footprint I recognise.
ZOOM on the scratched bark rising toward the treetop. SOUND: a distant owl calling.
CUT TO: RAVI pointing back toward the school lights as MINA packs away the torch.

The film script tells the camera exactly what to show and when, so I control which detail the audience notices first.

writing.title: Writing 4: A Letter from the Rescue Centre
writing.origin: Rebuilt from Grade 5 Unit 9 Lesson and Story sources
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Write a letter from Amal or Sami to the rest of the class about the most important thing they learned at Nookwatch.
Use at least four unit words, and support your main point with one detail taken from the story.
Finish with something clear that you want the class to do next.
writing.modelText:
Dear Class,
The most important thing I learned is that a rescue centre is nothing like a zoo. Talia told us that animals rarely show injury unless it is serious, so those abnormal footprints mattered far more than we realised.
Please join the informal patrol on Friday, because the fences still need checking.
writing.expectedLength: One letter of two organised paragraphs

items: Dear Class,

The most important thing I learned is that a wildlife rescue centre only steps in when an animal truly cannot manage alone. Talia explained that an informal check of the fence line found the scratched bark before the injury became serious, which showed me how much an abnormal sign like that actually matters.
Please help check the noticeboard map on Monday, because the reserve wants volunteers to mark every gap in the fence.
From Sami
otherAnswers: Writing as Amal instead of Sami works just as well, as long as the letter is signed with that name.
A different main lesson would also fit, such as how quietly a rescue team has to move, supported with a different detail from the story.

writing.successCriteria: I used a greeting and a sign-off; I named the most important thing I learned; I supported it with a detail from the story; I used at least four unit words; I organised my ideas into paragraphs; I checked my punctuation

writing.title: Writing 5: The Next Chapter

Back at Hilltop Primary the corridor smelled of wet coats. Amal pinned a poster beside the noticeboard while Sami held the drawing pins.

items: Back at Hilltop Primary the corridor still smelled of wet coats. Amal pinned a poster beside the noticeboard while Sami held the drawing pins steady, and Talia's warning about snares kept circling in her mind.

"What is a wildlife club actually for?" Nora asked, tilting her head at the poster. "It is for anyone who wants to check the school fence properly," Sami said, "because Talia showed us how one loose wire can trap an animal for days."

By the end of lunch nine names filled the sign-up sheet, and Amal already knew the first job: walking the fence line together on Saturday morning to look for exactly the abnormal marks Talia had taught them to spot.

grownUpGuide.label: Teacher & Parent Guide
grownUpGuide.intro: In this unit, your child works through "Lights, Camera, Action…" on their own — new words, a grammar focus, and a set of longer readings. This guide shows you what they are working on so you can talk about it with them.

sections.title: 🧭 About this unit (please read first)
sections.body:
Your child is about 9-10 years old and works through this unit largely on their own — reading, practising and checking answers at their own pace. Your role is different from the early grades: you keep them company from outside the screen rather than leading each page.

The most useful things you can do are also the simplest: ask what the unit's texts are about, listen to them read a paragraph aloud, hear the new words used in sentences, and read their writing when they submit it. A few minutes of real conversation about the unit turns silent screen work into language they can actually use.

This guide tells you what the unit covers so you can ask good questions without working through the pages yourself.

sections.title: 💬 Using the AI Tutor with your child
sections.body:
At this age your child can use the AI Tutor on their own — it is worth sitting in occasionally to see how they use it, and showing them what it can do.

Suggest they ask it to quiz them on this unit's words: "Ask me questions about the word 'nook'."

Suggest they paste in a sentence of their own and ask whether it sounds natural, and how to say it better.

Encourage 'why' questions — why a comma goes there, why the text says it that way. Asking the tutor to explain, not just to check, is where the learning is.

sections.title: 🌟 Tips for supporting this unit
sections.body:
Short, regular sessions still beat one long one. A unit spread over several days sticks; a unit crammed in one sitting does not.

Talk about the reading away from the screen — over a meal, in the car. Retelling a text in their own words is one of the strongest checks of understanding there is.

Treat their writing as a draft to improve, not an answer to mark. Pick one thing to praise and one thing to sharpen, and stop there.

Praise precision and persistence, not just speed. At this stage careful, complete answers matter more than quick ones.

sections.title: What Your Child Will Be Able to Do
items: Recognise the layout and features of a play script, including the cast list, character names, colons, dialogue and stage directions.
Explain the difference between a play script and a film script, using examples from both versions of “The Forest Guardians”.
Read stage directions accurately and locate upstage, downstage, centre stage and the entrances and exits they describe.
Understand and use drama and camera vocabulary such as pan, zoom, cut, close-up and point of view.
Identify, form and use compound nouns in sentences, and choose the closed, open or hyphenated form correctly.
Write a short play script scene with correct formatting: names in capitals, colons before dialogue and stage directions in brackets.
Perform a short script aloud, matching tone, expression and movement to the stage directions.
Use the unit's vocabulary precisely in speech and writing, including the words drawn from the Nookwatch story.

sections.title: How to Support This Unit, Step by Step
sections.body:
A simple shape for staying involved without taking over:

1. Before they start (2 min)
Skim this guide's word list and text titles so you know what to ask about later. You do not need to work through the pages yourself.

2. While they work
Let them work alone at their own pace. Be within reach for a word or an instruction they cannot crack, but resist doing the thinking for them.

3. Talk about the reading (5 min)
Ask them to tell you what "The Forest Guardians: a play script" was about in their own words, and what happened in "Nookwatch: The Forest Mission, part 1" — and what they thought of it.

4. Hear the words (5 min)
Pick a few words from the list below and ask for each one in a spoken sentence of their own. Saying a word out loud fixes it far better than reading it silently.

5. Check the grammar landed (3 min)
Ask them to explain "What a Compound Noun Is" to you as if you were the student. Teaching it back is the quickest way to find out whether it stuck.

6. Read their writing (5 min)
When the Writing section is submitted, read it together. Praise one specific thing, suggest one improvement, and leave it there.

items: No rule predicts the form. Many open compounds slowly close up as people use them more often, which is how 'to-day' turned into 'today'.
Stress carries meaning.
Notice that a single page can hold all three written forms at once.
The first word usually carries the stress.

sections.title: Simple Check — What to Look For
sections.body: You do not need a test. These are the signs the unit has landed — listen for them in conversation and look for them in the writing:
items: Learner labels a script page correctly and answers the script-feature comprehension questions.
Learner names at least two features unique to each version and justifies the difference.
Learner follows a bracketed direction on a marked stage plan and explains the position aloud.
Learner sorts directions into film or stage and uses three camera terms correctly in writing.
Learner sorts ten compounds by form and corrects five miswritten compounds in context.
Learner submits a scene of eight to twelve lines that meets every point on the writing checklist.
Learner records a performance in which voice and gesture follow the bracketed directions.
Learner uses at least eight unit words accurately across one written and one spoken task.
